analysis.one_liner: Makes large employers repay the government for workers' Medicaid and children's health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House member in September 2005, sent to a committee that never acted on it, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007 without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged large employers — companies with 50 or more workers — a fee whenever one of their full-time employees, or that employee's spouse or child, was enrolled in Medicaid or the children's health program (SCHIP). The fee would roughly match what the government spends to cover that person, and the money would go back to the state that paid for the coverage. The idea: companies that don't offer affordable health benefits shouldn't shift the cost of covering their workers onto taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, state Medicaid and SCHIP programs would have been repaid for covering workers whose employers don't provide health benefits, easing pressure to cut those programs or raise taxes. Workers at large companies that pay low wages and skip benefits would have had a strong reason for their employers to offer coverage instead. Taxpayers generally would have carried less of the cost of employer-driven poverty coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Charges employers with 50 or more workers a per-person fee, roughly 80% of the state's average monthly cost of covering an adult or child on Medicaid or SCHIP, when a full-time employee or that employee's spouse or child is enrolled in the program [S3].
Sends the collected money back to the state that actually provided the Medicaid or SCHIP coverage, so the program that paid the bill gets reimbursed [S3].
Applies to employees working at least 40 hours a week for at least three months, targeting full-time workforces rather than part-time staffing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — big retail chains, service companies, and other firms with 50 or more employees — that rely on public coverage for their workers' families would have paid a fee for each covered person each quarter. Some of that cost could have been passed to consumers through prices, or avoided by employers offering health benefits, raising wages, or cutting staff hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large low-wage employers without health benefits

drawbacks.text: Employers could have responded in ways that hurt workers instead of helping them: cutting hours below the 40-hour threshold, avoiding hires, or shifting costs into lower wages, since the bill penalizes employment of workers who end up on public coverage [S3].

The fee applies per covered person each month with no offset for employers who already contribute to employee health plans, and its formula tracks state average costs rather than what any individual employer's benefits are worth, which supporters of a lighter mandate would call too blunt [S3].
Some of the employer cost would likely reach consumers and shareholders through prices and reduced profits, not only in changed behavior at the workplace [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real cost shift: large, profitable companies using taxpayer-funded coverage as a substitute for benefits. Its main weakness is design — a blunt per-person fee with a 40-hour cutoff invites employers to cut hours or shift pay to dodge it, and there was no carve-out for firms that already help pay for insurance. A well-designed version could have recovered public money and nudged employers toward offering coverage; this version's incentives for workers on the margin of full-time status were a genuine cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never considered it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on September 27, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the referral was the bill's only action [S5].
The bill carried 13 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican cosponsor [S4].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died with it, a routine fate for the large majority of bills that never get a committee vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers that would have owed the fee are better off, because no cost was ever imposed. State Medicaid and SCHIP programs — and the taxpayers backing them — continue absorbing the cost of covering workers whose employers don't provide health benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers that would have paid the fee

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (big-box retail, food service, service chains)
industries.note: The bill would have charged them a quarterly fee for every full-time worker, spouse, or child on Medicaid or SCHIP, ending a free ride on public coverage. Their alternative — offering benefits or raising pay — is what the bill aimed to force. Sources: [S3].
States would have been reimbursed for coverage costs driven by employers' benefit decisions, easing pressure to cut benefits or raise taxes. Sources: [S3].
